questions.question: The work done on an object by a force is calculated as:
options: FΔx cos θ — force times displacement times the cosine of the angle between them
FΔt — force times the contact time

questions.question: A very large force acting at 90° to an object's displacement does:
options: A very large amount of work

questions.question: A gardener drags a compost bag 8 m with a horizontal force of 60 N. The work done by the applied force is:
Friction of 25 N acts on the bag over the same 8 m. The work done by friction is:

subtopics.title: Net Work from the Free-Body Diagram

questions.question: Two valid routes to the net work on an object are:
options: Adding force magnitudes, or multiplying mass by displacement
Summing each force's work with signs, or applying FnetΔx cos θ once
Using only the largest force, or only friction
Averaging the positive and negative forces

questions.question: For the bag pulled with 60 N against 25 N of friction over 8 m, the net work is:
Positive net work done on an object tells you that the object:
options: Speeds up — energy is flowing into its motion

questions.question: For an object dragged at constant velocity, the net work over the journey is:
options: Positive and proportional to the distance
Equal to the work of the applied force
Zero — positive and negative contributions cancel

questions.question: The work-energy theorem equates the net work done on an object to:
options: The change in its kinetic energy
The impulse of the net force

questions.question: A net work of 280 J is done on a 15 kg bag starting from rest. Its final speed is closest to:
A 1 200 kg bakkie at 25 m·s⁻¹ brakes to rest in 62,5 m. The average friction force is:
The work-energy theorem is the natural tool when a question supplies:
options: A distance over which forces act

questions.question: On a slope of angle θ, the component of the weight directed ALONG the slope is:
A 25 kg crate is pulled up a 30° ramp at constant velocity against 35 N of friction. The applied force parallel to the ramp is:
Over 6 m up the ramp, the work done by gravity on the crate is:
Because the crate moves at constant velocity, the net work over the 6 m must be:
options: Zero, since the kinetic energy does not change
945 J, the work of the applied force
Equal to the normal force times 6 m

questions.question: Holding a 25 kg crate of tiles perfectly still for five minutes does:
options: A large amount of work, because it is tiring
Zero work on the crate, because there is no displacement
Work equal to the crate's weight times the time

questions.question: Carrying the crate along a level corridor at constant height does zero work on it because:
options: The crate moves at constant speed
The upward carrying force is perpendicular to the horizontal motion
The crate's mass stays the same

questions.question: Lowering the crate gently to the floor, your hands do:
options: Negative work — the upward force opposes the downward motion

questions.question: In the bank account picture of this lesson, the balance stands for the object's:
Doubling a minibus's speed multiplies its kinetic energy by:
options: Four — kinetic energy grows with the square of the speed

questions.question: With the same braking force, a vehicle travelling at twice the speed needs:
A question that gives you a stopping DISTANCE is pointing you toward:
Compared with lifting a drum straight up, rolling it up a long gentle plank to the same height needs:
options: Less force and less total work
Less force but the same total work against gravity
The same force over a shorter distance

questions.question: The work done against gravity in reaching the trailer depends on:
options: The vertical height gained, not the length of the plank
The length of the plank alone

questions.question: A long gentle plank can cost MORE total energy than a short steep one because friction:
options: Charges per metre of surface travelled

questions.question: Rolling the drum up the plank at constant speed means the energy you supplied went into:
options: Nothing, since the speed never changed
Height gained and heat from friction, with no change in kinetic energy
